Shiue and Shiue (2014) estimated that 9% of hypertension cases in Scotland could be attributed to indoor temperatures below 18°C. 2. Respiratory Health and Indoor Temperature: Children with asthma experienced small but measurable declines in lung function when exposed to indoor temperatures below 12°C, as reported by Pierse et al. (2013). Bedroom temperatures had a stronger impact on lung function than living room temperatures. Ross et al. (1990) found no significant association between upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) in children and indoor temperatures. However, children who wheezed were more likely to sleep in cooler bedrooms and live in homes with open fires rather than central heating. The authors suggested that cooler bedroom temperatures might contribute to wheezing in children. 3. Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD): Osman et al. (2008) reported that COPD patients living in colder homes had worse health outcomes, including more severe symptoms and greater activity limitations. Homes often failed to maintain recommended temperatures of 21°C in living rooms and 18°C in bedrooms. Smokers with COPD were particularly affected by colder indoor environments. 4. Biomarkers and Indoor Temperature: These biomarkers showed linear associations with room temperature, indicating that colder environments may contribute to adverse health outcomes (Shiue, 2016). 5. Limitations and Confounding Factors: Many studies did not account for all potential confounding factors, such as socioeconomic status, smoking, alcohol consumption, and housing quality. For example, Shiue and Shiue (2014) noted that wide confidence intervals for temperatures below 16°C limited the precision of their findings. Some studies, such as Ross et al. (1990), were small and localized, raising questions about their generalizability to broader populations. 6. Recommendations: Maintaining indoor temperatures above 18°C is recommended to reduce the risk of hypertension and other adverse health outcomes. For vulnerable populations, such as the elderly and individuals with chronic respiratory conditions, higher temperatures (e.g., 21°C in living rooms) may be beneficial. In conclusion, the evidence highlights the importance of maintaining adequate indoor temperatures to support cardiovascular and respiratory health, particularly in colder climates. Public health interventions targeting indoor heating may help mitigate health risks associated with cold homes.
